To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the contribution to international inequality in emissions per capita of affluence is positive, that of demographic factors is negative, that of sectoral composition is positive, and that of climate is negligible.

1) The contribution of the demographic factors to inequality in CO2 per capita is significant, though decreasing; 2) The contribution of affluency to CO2 inequality is significant, and has been increasing; 3) The contribution of sectoral structure of CO2 per capita has been significant, but it has been decreasing; 4) The contribution of climate is significant, but it is not increasing.

(1) the contribution of demographic variables is significant; (2) the share of affluence is significant; (3) the contribution of the industrial and service sectors is negative, whereas the share of energy consumption is positive.

the contribution of different causal factors to international inequality, and not with the inequality itself.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the contribution of affluency and sectoral composition to emissions inequality has been decreasing in the past years, while the contribution of demographic and climatic factors has been increasing.
the contribution of affluent countries to the overall inequality in CO2 per capita is significant and has been decreasing in the period studied.
the most significant factors in explaining inequality in emissions per capita are affluence and the composition of the economy.
